opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. There's a really important dynamic: the frontier models keep getting more capable, and then a lot of that capability gets distilled into much smaller, cheaper models that are good enough for a huge fraction of what people do today. That's great, and we invest heavily in it, because serving cost and latency matter enormously when you're deploying something to billions of users.

But I don't think "good enough for today's tasks" means we should stop pushing. One reason is that the set of tasks people attempt is shaped by what the models can do. As models get more capable, people start asking them to do things they never would have tried a year earlier: longer multi-step agentic work, writing and debugging substantial chunks of software, reasoning over enormous amounts of context, doing real scientific work. The demand curve moves with the capability curve.

The second reason is that the frontier is what makes the cheap models good in the first place. Distillation works really well when you have a very capable teacher. If you stop advancing the large models, the small models plateau too. So I see them as complementary: the big model pushes the frontier, and then you compress that into something you can serve at very low cost and latency.

And third, there's a whole tail of really valuable problems, in healthcare, materials science, and education, where we're still well short of what would be genuinely transformative. Being a bit more reliable or a bit better at reasoning on those can matter enormously, even if most everyday queries are already handled well.

So my view is that you want a whole Pareto frontier of models: very capable ones where quality matters most, and very efficient ones where cost and speed dominate. You keep pushing both ends at once.

r001.rationale: The response says that as models become more capable, people ask them to do tasks they would not previously have attempted, including longer multi-step work and substantial software tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two things are actually complementary rather than in tension. Historically, what we've seen is that every time we push the frontier of what the most capable model can do, that capability tends to trickle down into much smaller and cheaper models within a year or two. So the frontier model today is sort of a preview of what the "good enough" cheap model will be next year. Distillation, better training recipes, better data, all of those things mean the expensive capability becomes inexpensive capability pretty quickly.

So I don't think of the frontier as being about the tasks people are doing today. The tasks people do today are, almost by definition, the tasks that current models can already do reasonably well. The interesting question is what tasks people aren't doing because no model can do them yet. If you can get a model to reason over a problem for hours instead of seconds, or to work reliably on a codebase of millions of lines, or to actually contribute to scientific research in a meaningful way, those aren't things anyone is asking a cheap model to do right now, because it wouldn't work. Once it does work, that's a whole new class of use cases, and then the cost curve applies again.

The other thing I'd say is that the economics are a little bit different than people assume. A lot of the cost of a model is in training, and that's amortized across an enormous number of uses. The inference cost is what people see, and we've been driving that down by orders of magnitude over a few years, through better hardware, better serving systems, things like speculative decoding, and smarter architectures where you don't have to activate the entire model for every token. So it's not that you pick between capable and cheap. You push capability, and then you spend a lot of effort making that capability cheap, and you repeat.

And honestly, "good enough for people's current tasks" is a bit of a moving target. People's expectations rise. A few years ago, a model that could write a coherent paragraph was remarkable. Now if it makes a mistake in a long document, people are annoyed. That's a healthy dynamic. It means there's still a lot of headroom in reliability, in long-horizon work, in handling things like video and code and the physical world together. I don't think we're anywhere near the point where more capability stops being useful.

r001.rationale: The response says that as models become capable of tasks they cannot handle today, a new class of use cases becomes possible, and that people’s expectations rise. This communicates that greater capability leads users to pursue more complex tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think “good enough” is always relative to what you’re asking the model to do. If you have a particular task and a smaller, cheaper model does it reliably, that’s great. You want to use that model, and making those capabilities cheaper means many more people can use them.

But the set of tasks people ask models to do isn’t fixed. People adapt their requests to what the models can handle. If a model struggles with something, you might stop asking it to do that, or break the problem into little pieces and do a lot of the work yourself. So looking only at people’s current usage can underestimate the value of better capabilities.

For example, getting help with a few lines of code is useful. Being able to hand over a much larger programming task and have the model carry it through reliably would be useful in a different way. That requires more capability, even if the cheaper model is already perfectly adequate for completing those few lines.

So I see these as complementary directions: make existing capabilities much more efficient, and push forward on what’s possible. Better capabilities open up new uses, and efficiency makes those uses broadly accessible.

r001.rationale: It says people adapt their requests to what models can handle and gives the example of handing a model a much larger programming task as capabilities improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “good enough” is always relative to the task you’re trying to do. If you hold the task fixed, then having a smaller, cheaper model that does it well is incredibly valuable. You can make that capability available to more people, with lower latency, and use it in places where the economics didn’t work before.

But people’s tasks aren’t fixed. When models become more capable, people start asking them to do things they wouldn’t have considered asking before. Instead of helping you write one function, maybe they can help you understand a large codebase or carry out a more substantial engineering task. Those require a different level of capability and reliability.

So I think both directions matter. You want to keep pushing what’s possible, and you want to make existing capabilities dramatically more efficient. And those reinforce each other: something that requires a frontier model today can become a much cheaper, broadly available capability later.

r001.rationale: The response says that as models become more capable, people ask them to do things they would not have considered before, such as moving from writing one function to understanding a large codebase or doing substantial engineering work.
